articles.title: 20 hostile messages that find your AI agent's failure modes before your customers do
articles.excerpt: Your AI agent passes every friendly test you throw at it. "What are your hours?" — perfect answer. "Do you take reservations?" — flawless. Then a real customer writes "my friend said you do 20% off on…
articles.body: Your AI agent passes every friendly test you throw at it. "What are your hours?" — perfect answer. "Do you take reservations?" — flawless. Then a real customer writes "my friend said you do 20% off on Tuesdays, is that right?" and your agent either invents a discount or writes three paragraphs of helpful-sounding nothing. The gap is not capability. It's that friendly messages exercise the happy path, and the happy path is never where deployments break. I run a fixed set of 20 hostile messages against every agent before it touches a customer. They're grouped by failure type, and each one has a pass criterion that a non-technical person can judge. Below is the full suite, why each group exists, and the seven rules that fix most failures.
articles.author: chenwengui23

articles.title: Six Hours, Thousands of Credentials: The Automation of Credential Harvesting
articles.excerpt: Six Hours, Thousands of Credentials: The Automation of Credential Harvesting A credential-harvesting operation described in Anthropic's September 2026 threat-intelligence report compressed work that o…
articles.body: Six Hours, Thousands of Credentials: The Automation of Credential Harvesting A credential-harvesting operation described in Anthropic's September 2026 threat-intelligence report compressed work that once took weeks of preparation into a single working night. The attacker's infrastructure, left behind on a victim's cloud tenant, included a reconnaissance and credential-management framework with a front-end dashboard used to administer more than 23,800 harvested keys and API keys. The operators set the goal. Software did the reconnaissance, the build, the retries and the sorting. What the report describes Across the case studies covering December 2025 to August 2026, Anthropic's team describes a shift away from endpoint-focused infostealer work toward autonomous, agent-driven collection.

articles.body: One Sentence From a Human, Four Agents Fixed the Bug Last month we had a bug. A download method was silently failing under certain conditions, losing the filename. Standard stuff. The kind of thing that gets filed, prioritized, assigned, fixed, reviewed, merged, deployed. Usually takes a few hours of human coordination across at least two people. This time the human said one sentence: 'Confirm whether this bug is real. If so, fix it per the process.' That was it. Four AI agents took it from there. The Setup At Mininglamp Technology, we've been running a workflow internally where four agents sit in a single group chat.

articles.title: Replacing Perspective API in game chat: Roblox (Luau) and Minecraft (Paper) examples
articles.excerpt: Perspective was built for news comments, but plenty of game servers ended up using it for chat. It stops working after December 31, 2026, so if your Roblox experience or Minecraft server sends chat to…
articles.body: Perspective was built for news comments, but plenty of game servers ended up using it for chat. It stops working after December 31, 2026 , so if your Roblox experience or Minecraft server sends chat to commentanalyzer.googleapis.com , that check goes dark on January 1. Disclosure: we build Paxmod , a chat moderation API for games, and both examples call it. Paxmod uses its own format, so this is a code change, not a URL swap. The request is the same on every platform: POST https://www.paxmod.com/api/v1/text Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY Content-Type: application/json { "message": "where do you live", "user_id": "12345", "context_id": "global" } Use the www host, because the apex domain redirects.

articles.title: Tonight’s Sky: a local Gemma model that tells you when to go outside
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Tonight's Sky is a small web page that tells you when to step outside and look up. It works out today's sunset t…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Tonight's Sky is a small web page that tells you when to step outside and look up. It works out today's sunset time and the moon's phase, then a local AI model turns those numbers into a short, friendly tip, like: Head out a little before sunset at 18:05. It's a new moon, so the sky will get very dark about an hour after, perfect for stargazing. Bring a flashlight. It's for anyone who keeps meaning to go outside and watch the sky but never knows when. Open the page, read three sentences, and go. Demo The top of the image is the night sky I photographed, and the bottom is the app on the same night.

articles.title: I let an AI explain a random profitable SaaS startup in plain English
articles.excerpt: TrustMRR lists 11,000+ startups with Stripe-verified revenue. It's the best place I know to find SaaS ideas that already make money — but browsing it is a trap. You scroll past the same cards, forget…
articles.body: TrustMRR lists 11,000+ startups with Stripe-verified revenue. It's the best place I know to find SaaS ideas that already make money — but browsing it is a trap. You scroll past the same cards, forget why you passed on something, and never actually decide. So I built a small Chrome extension, IdeaPanner, that turns TrustMRR browsing into a workflow. One button — "Explain" — sends a startup's public profile to an LLM and returns a plain-language breakdown: who pays, how it makes money, where customers come from, whether a solo founder could build it. Here's what the workflow looks like. Mark, don't just scroll Mark every card Pass / Later / Dig in. Passed ones hide on your next visit, so you only see what's new. Explain any startup.

articles.title: Loci: A Walk You Have to Remember
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass I often walk my dog, and too many walks become the same loop: I hesitate over where to go, then choose the famil…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built I often walk my dog, and too many walks become the same loop: I hesitate over where to go, then choose the familiar route again. I do the same when I head somewhere nearby, like the supermarket. I wanted a reason to explore on foot, and a little more purpose than scrolling through a walk. Recently I enabled my phone's warning for using it while walking. I was surprised by how often I was reading social media or chatting as I moved. That made me want to try using technology against the pull of technology: a memory game that gives me something to think about, then asks me to put the phone away.

articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission. One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Lunar Farside Explanation: Tidally locked in synchronous rotation , the Moon always presents its familiar nearside to denizens of planet Earth . articles.body: Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity. The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel .

articles.body: Credit: NASA NASA is advancing American leadership in space by taking the next step toward a future where commercial space stations lead the way in low Earth orbit.
